<teammate-message teammate_id="team-lead" summary="Research HAAS classic control UI">
Research the HAAS CNC classic control (pre-NGC, the green-screen control used on VF-series mills, as seen on older HAAS pendants) using WebSearch and WebFetch. Do NOT write any files — web reading only.

I'm planning a web-based "HAAS lookalike" trainer UI for students (a g-code sender skinned as a HAAS control), so I need accurate details of the UI and its operation:

1. Screen/display pages: what pages exist behind the DISPLAY key group (PROGRAM, POSITION, OFFSET, CURR COMDS, ALARMS, PARAM/DGNOS, SETNG/GRAPH, HELP/CALC) and roughly what each page shows and its layout. The classic UI: green background, layout of panes (program pane, position pane, spindle pane, timers, etc.).
2. Mode keys and behavior: EDIT, MEM, MDI/DNC, HANDLE JOG, ZERO RET, LIST PROG — what each mode does and how the operator flow works (e.g., select program in LIST PROG, run in MEM with CYCLE START, MDI entry, jog increments .0001/.001/.01/.1, zero return ALL/SINGLE/ORIGIN/HOME G28).
3. Keypad groups and key functions: cursor keys, alpha/numeric entry style (e.g., typing program O numbers, offsets entry with F1/PART ZERO SET/TOOL OFSET MESUR), overrides section (feedrate +10%/-10%/100%, spindle, rapid 5%/25%/50%/100%, spindle CW/CCW/STOP), jog keys, COOLNT key.
4. Position display: the four position readouts (OPERATOR, WORK G54, MACHINE, DIST TO GO) and POSIT page behavior.
5. Offsets: tool length offsets page, work offsets (G54-G59, G154 Pxx) page layout and how values are entered.
6. Typical color scheme and fonts of the classic control screen (green background, white/yellow/cyan text areas) — enough detail to recreate the look.
7. Any existing HAAS control simulators/trainers (commercial or open source) worth knowing about.

Return a structured, concrete summary organized by topic. Include layout details wherever sources describe them.
</teammate-message>

 Introduction to Basic Vertical Mill Operation
Welcome to Productivity, Inc., your local Haas Factory Outlet (H.F.O.) for the Haas Mill Operator Class.
This class is intended to give a basic understanding of the set-up and operation of a Haas Machining
Center.
After 1945 design of wings for the US Air Force were becoming extremely complex and hard to
manufacture using conventional machine tools. MIT developed a machine that was able to control a
cutting tool path with a series of straight lines defined by axial coordinates at prescribed feed rates.
The first NC machine tool was introduced to the defense and aerospace industry by MIT in 1952. The
contour of a constantly changing curvature could be described by a series of short lines determined by a
series of coordinate in three axes.
The first machine tools were run with instructions or programs punched out on paper tape. The files of
the early machine tools were often in the format which later became called G-code. The reason for the
name being that many of the lines of text began the letter G.

supervision and with a great deal of repeatability. "CNC" (Computerized Numerical Control) is the same
type of operating system, with the exception that a computer monitors the machine tool.
The same principles used in operating a manual machine are used in programming a NC or CNC
Machine. The main difference is that instead of cranking handles to position a slide to a certain point,
the dimension is stored in the memory of the machine control once. The control will then move the
machine to these positions each time the program is run.
The operation of the VF-Series Vertical Machining Center requires that a part program be designed,
written, and entered into the memory of the control. There are several options for getting these
programs to the control. RS-232 (serial port with a computer), 3.5” Floppy Disk, Ethernet / Networking/
and USB are all viable ways to transmit and receive programs.
In order to operate and program a CNC controlled machine, a basic understanding of machining
practices and a working knowledge of math are necessary. It is also important to become familiar with
the control console and the placement of the keys, switches, displays, etc., that are pertinent to the
operation of the machine.
This manual can be used as both an operator's manual and as a programmer's manual. It is intended to
give a basic understanding of CNC programming and its applications. It is not intended as an in-depth
study of all ranges of machine use, but as an overview of common and potential situations facing CNC
programmers. Much more training and information is necessary before attempting to program on the
machine.
The programming section of this manual is meant as a supplementary teaching aid to users of the HAAS
Vertical Machining Center. The information in this section may apply in whole or in part to the operation
of other CNC machines. Its use is intended only as an aid in the operation of the HAAS Vertical
Machining Center.

Absolute Positioning:

The machine illustration shows three directions of travel available on a vertical machine center. Now to
carry the number line idea a little further, imagine such a line placed along each set of travels (or axis) of

move the spindle to the right on our part, and negative would move the spindle to the left.
If we place a similar number line along the front-to-back, or “Y” axis, and wanted to move the spindle to
the back of the table, these would be positive values. Moving the spindle towards the operator would
be negative values in the Y axis.
The third axis of travel on our machine is the up-and-down, or “Z” axis. A positive Z value will move the
spindle up towards the tool change position, and negative values would move the spindle towards our
part.

# Haas Mill Classic Control: Objectives & Glossary

## Class Objectives

The course aims to enable learners to:

1. "Compare the Classic Haas Control to other Haas CNC controls"
2. "Describe the Classic Haas Control"
3. "Identify the different areas of the Classic Haas Control"
4. Distinguish between display, operation mode, and function keys
5. "Identify the location of the alpha and numeric keys"
6. Understand special characters and override functions
7. Locate cursor and jog keys on the control keypad
8. "Differentiate between function keys on the Classic Haas Control"
9. Explain powering up/down sequences and zero return mode
10. "Demonstrate knowledge of the coolant activating process"
11. Describe chip conveyor activation and message-leaving procedures

---

## Key Components Glossary

### Display Keys
Located in the top center of the control keypad:
- **ALARM/MESGS** - Shows current alerts or messages
- **CURNT COMDS** - Displays fifteen program lines with axis positions
- **HELP/CALC** - Provides instructional content and machining calculators
- **OFFSET** - Shows programmed offset values
- **POSIT** - Lists spindle axis positions across multiple pages
- **PRGRM/CONVRS** - Displays current program blocks
- **SETNG/GRAPH** - Lists settings or dry run information
- **PARAM/DGNOS** - Shows machine parameters or diagnostic data

### Operation Mode Keys
Determine which machine tasks execute:
- **EDIT** - "allows manual editing of a program or the creation of new program"
- **HAND JOG** - Enables manual tool movement via dial or buttons
- **LIST PROG** - "lists programs and allows an operator to select, send, receive, and delete"
- **MDI/DNC** - Executes manual data input or centralized computer programs
- **MEM** - "runs part programs from the control's memory"
- **ZERO RET** - "searches for machine zero or rapid returns to machine zero"

### Function Keys
Located in the upper left corner:
- **NEXT TOOL** - Selects subsequent tool after offset measurement
- **PART ZERO SET** - "automatically enter work coordinate offsets during part setup"
- **TOOL OFSET MESUR** - "enter the present Z location for the tool length offsets"
- **TOOL RELEASE** - Removes tool from spindle in MDI, HAND JOG, or ZERO RETURN modes

### Override Keys
Located in lower left, adjust speeds/feeds during operation:
- **Speed Controls** - CW, CCW, STOP, ±10 SPINDLE, 100% SPINDLE
- **Feed Controls** - ±10 FEED RATE, 100% FEED RATE, HAND CNTRL FEED
- **Rapid Controls** - 5%, 25%, 50%, 100% RAPID, HAND CNTRL SPIN

### Jog Keys
Enable spindle movement along axes:
- **Axis Movement** - +X, -X, +Y, -Y, +Z, -Z (±A for optional fourth axis)
- **Chip Management** - CHIP FWD, CHIP REV, CHIP STOP
- **Coolant Control** - AUX CLNT, CLNT UP, CLNT DOWN
- **Continuous Jogging** - JOG LOCK

### Cursor Keys
Allow navigation through screens and programs:
- **Arrow Keys** - Navigate up, down, left, right
- **PAGE UP/DOWN** - Move one page in displays or program
- **HOME** - Jump to beginning; **END** - Jump to end

### Reset Keys
Located in upper left corner, execute vital startup/shutdown functions:
- **POWER UP/RESTART** - "automatically initializes the machine at power up"
- **RESET** - "stops all machine motion and places the program cursor at the top"
- **TOOL CHANGER RESTORE** - "restores the tool changer to normal operation"
- **POWER ON/OFF** - Green button enables; red button disables machine

---

## Important Control Panel Elements

**Display Screen** - Main interface showing operator information
**Input Buffer** - Temporary holding area at lower left for incoming data
**HANDLE** - Rotating knob for axis-specific movement in controlled increments
**SPINDLE LOAD meter** - Indicates power draw during operations
**EMERGENCY STOP** - Immediately halts all functions during emergencies

# Summary of Offsets Display and Current Commands Display

Based on the Haas Mill Operator's Manual (Page 25), here are the key sections:

## Offsets Display

The manual describes two offset pages:

The manual lists several Current Command pages accessible via the Current Commands button:

2. **Current Display Command:** Presents "current program codes and their current value" (read-only).

3. **Macro Variables Display:** Lists "macro variables and their present values," which update as programs run and can be modified by operators.

# Alarms/Messages Display Summary

Based on the Haas Mill Operator's Manual page 26, here's what the documentation covers:

## Alarms Display

The alarm function is accessed via the ALARM/MESGS button and provides three viewing modes:

1. **Current Alarms Screen** - Shows any active alarms
2. **Alarm History Screen** - Displays previously received alarms (accessed via Right Arrow)
3. **Alarm Viewer Screen** - Shows individual alarms with descriptions, allowing users to scroll through entries or search by alarm number

Users can navigate through alarms using cursor keys, Page Up/Down, and other navigation buttons.

Accessed by pressing ALARM/MESGS twice, this feature provides an "operator message display" with no operational impact on the control. Operators can input custom messages using the keypad, with space and cancel buttons available for editing. The system retains message data persistently, even after power cycles, and displays the message page during startup if no active alarms exist.

## Additional Monitoring Features

The manual also describes related displays including operation timers, tool life tracking, tool load monitoring, and axis load assessment—all accessible through the control's display interface to help operators manage machine performance and maintenance.

# Haas Mill Classic Controls: Entering Offsets 260

## Class Objectives

The course covers 15 learning objectives including:

- Understanding offset purposes and types available on Haas mills
- Distinguishing between work offsets, tool length offsets, and wear offsets
- Navigating offset displays and menus
- Changing work offsets and tool length offsets manually
- Using the "TOOL OFFSET MEASURE feature" to adjust tool lengths
- Managing cutter compensation and wear offsets
- Enabling coolant offsets and clearing all offsets

## Key Glossary Terms

**Work Offset**: "An offset used to adjust the location of every tool loaded in the machine. On the mill, the work offset changes the position of the spindle in both the X and Y axes, and often the Z axis as well."

**Tool Length Offset**: "An offset used on the mill that accounts for variations in tool length along the Z axis."

**TOOL OFFSET MEASURE**: "A function key that is used to enter the current Z axis location for the tool length offsets in the offset page during part setup."

**Wear Offset**: "An offset that allows for the slight adjustment of the cutter location in all three axes."

**Cutter Compensation Offset**: "An offset used on the mill that accounts for variations in tool diameter."

**OFFSET Key**: "The display key on the Haas control that shows the various programmed offsets."

**Coolant Offset**: "An offset that controls the position of the coolant spigot on some Haas machines."

# Haas Mill Classic Controls: Program Execution Objectives & Glossary

## Class Objectives

The course aims to develop these competencies:

- Explain the connection between part programs and Haas control systems
- Locate the active program using proper control keys
- Execute programs using the Haas control interface
- Distinguish between normal and abnormal program stops
- Perform mid-sequence program restarts within toolpaths
- Utilize the Run-Stop-Jog-Continue operational feature
- Access and review programs during execution
- Run programs through graphics visualization mode
- Search for specific program codes
- Remove unwanted programs from the system

## Key Glossary Terms

**CYCLE START**: "The button used to begin a program or continue a program that has been previously stopped"

**FEED HOLD**: "The control used to pause a program. FEED HOLD pauses tool feed but does not stop spindle movement"

**SINGLE BLOCK**: "A key that, when pressed, causes only one block of a part program to be executed for each press of the CYCLE START button"

**Graphics Display**: "A function of the Haas control that allows an operator to visually dry run a part program without moving the axes"

**MEM Mode**: Referenced as the operational mode for program selection and execution

**Program Restart (Setting 36)**: "A setting on the Haas control that allows an operator to start a program from the middle of a tool sequence"

**Normal Stop**: "A regular means of halting a part program during the machining process"

**Run-Stop-Jog-Continue**: Enables interrupting execution, repositioning, and resuming operations

# Haas Mill Power-Up Procedure

Based on page 38 of the Haas Mill Operator's Manual, here is the machine power-up process:

## Initial Power-On
The operator starts the machine by "pressing the Power-On button on the pendant." The system then runs self-diagnostics and displays either a Messages screen or Alarms screen.

## Clearing Alarms
Upon startup, the mill typically shows "one alarm present (102 SERVOS OFF)." The operator clears this by "Pressing the Reset button a couple times." If alarms cannot be cleared, the manual notes the machine may require servicing.

## Homing the Machine
To establish the reference point needed for operations, the operator presses the "Power-Up Restart button." The manual warns that "Automatic motion will begin once this button is pressed" and advises keeping clear of the machine interior and tool changer. This button automatically clears alarm 102 if present.

# Haas Lathe Classic Control Panel: Objectives & Glossary

## Class Objectives

The course aims to develop operator competency across these key areas:

1. **Control Comparison & Description**: "Compare the Classic Haas CNC Control to other Haas CNC controls" and understand its structure and distinct regions.

2. **Panel Navigation**: Identify control areas and differentiate between display key functions (top and bottom rows), cursor key locations, and operation modes.

3. **Key Functions**: Understand override keys, alpha/numeric keypads, special characters, jog keys, function keys, and reset key operations.

4. **Practical Operations**: Demonstrate proficiency with power-up/power-down sequences, zero return mode, coolant activation, chip conveyor operation, and message creation.

## Display Keys Glossary

| Key | Definition |
|-----|-----------|
| **ALARM/MESGS** | "The display key on the Haas control that shows the current alarms when pressed once and messages when pressed twice." |
| **CURNT COMDS** | Shows fifteen program lines, modal values, axis positions, and runtime data |
| **OFSET** | Displays various programmed offsets |
| **POSIT** | Brings up different pages listing machine axis turret positions |
| **PRGRM/CONVRS** | "causes program blocks of the current selected part program to display" |
| **HELP/CALC** | Information manual and machining calculators |
| **PARAM/DGNOS** | Machine parameters and diagnostic information |
| **SETNG/GRAPH** | Settings and dry-run information |

## Operation Mode Keys

| Key | Function |
|-----|----------|
| **EDIT** | "allows manual editing changes in a part program or the creation of a new program in memory" |
| **HAND JOG** | Enables manual tool movement via handwheel or jog buttons |
| **LIST PROG** | Lists, selects, sends, receives, and deletes programs |
| **MDI/DNC** | Allows operator data entry and execution |
| **MEM** | Runs part programs from control memory |
| **ZERO RET** | Searches or rapidly returns to machine zero |

## Function Keys

| Key | Purpose |
|-----|---------|
| **NEXT TOOL** | Indexes turret for next tool during setup |
| **X DIA MESUR** | Records X-axis tool length offsets |
| **X/Z** | Toggles between X and Z axis jog modes |
| **Z FACE MESUR** | Records Z-axis tool length offsets |

## Override Keys

**Feedrate Controls**: Adjust tool feed in increments via -10, +10, and 100% buttons

**Spindle Controls**: Alter spindle speed in 10% increments through -10, +10, and 100% options

**Rapid Controls**: Adjust rapid traversal at 5%, 25%, 50%, or 100% rates

**Handle Controls**: 
- "allows the operator to adjust the programmed feed rate in 1% increments"
- "allows the operator to adjust spindle speed in 1% increments"

**Coolant Override (Setting 32)**: "controls how the coolant pump operates" and enables manual on/off capability

**STOP Key**: "discontinues an operation" and turns off spindle rotation

## Cursor Keys

| Key | Function |
|-----|----------|
| **HOME** | "moves a cursor quickly to its beginning" |
| **END** | Moves program quickly to its end |
| **PAGE UP** | Moves up one display or program page |
| **PAGE DOWN** | Changes displays or moves down one program page |
| **Arrow Keys** | Navigate up, down, left, and right through screens |

## Jog Keys

**Axis Movement**:
- **+X/-X**: "moves the turret along the X axis in the positive/negative direction"
- **+Z/-Z**: Moves turret along Z axis in positive/negative direction

**Coolant Nozzle**:
- **CLNT UP**: "incrementally raises the coolant nozzle"
- **CLNT DOWN**: Moves nozzle one position lower
- **AUX CLNT**: "turns on the through-spindle coolant system when in MDI mode"

**Chip Management**:
- **CHIP FWD**: Causes chip auger to remove chips
- **CHIP REV**: Rotates auger opposite the removal direction
- **CHIP STOP**: Halts auger rotation

**Tailstock**:
- **TS left/right arrows**: Feed tailstock at selected rate
- **TS RAPID**: Moves tailstock at maximum travel rate

## Alpha & Numeric Keys

**Alpha Keys**: Located in "bottom center of the control keypad" for letter and special character input

**Numeric Keys**: Positioned in "bottom right corner" for number and special character entry

**SPACE**: Adds spacing between characters

## Special Character Keys & Reset Functions

| Key | Function |
|-----|----------|
| **WRITE/ENTER** | Acts as enter key; functions as insert during editing |
| **CANCEL** | "backspaces the cursor to delete the last character entered" |
| **EOB** | Signals end of program block (semicolon) |
| **ORIGIN** | Resets highlighted values to zero |
| **AUTO OFF** | "automatically positions axes to machine zero and prepares the machine for power down" |
| **POWER UP/RESTART** | "automatically initializes the machine at power up" |
| **RESET** | Stops machine motion; places cursor at program top |

## Manual Controls

**EMERGENCY STOP**: "automatically shuts down all machine functions" for urgent/unsafe situations

**FEED HOLD**: Pauses program while maintaining spindle rotation

**HANDLE JOG**: Rotating knob enabling controlled, measured-increment axis movement

**POWER ON**: Green button providing machine power

**POWER OFF**: Red button shutting down machine power

## Display Screen

The screen presents all operational information needed during machining, including axis positions, program data, alarms, and system settings for operator reference during part production.

# Haas Mill Operator's Manual - Page 44 Summary

This page covers three key file management and control features:

## Disk Directory
The manual explains how to generate a directory listing of files on a floppy disk using the PRGM/LIST PROG mode and F4 key. The listing is automatically saved to a default program (O08999) that can be viewed in edit mode.

## File Delete
Users can delete files from a floppy disk by typing "DEL <filename>" on the List Prog page and pressing WRITE, which triggers a confirmation message before deletion.

## Direct Numeric Control (DNC)
DNC allows running programs as they arrive through the RS-232 port without size limitations, as the control executes code in real-time rather than storing it. Key points include:

- Enabled via Parameter 57 bit 18 and Setting 55
- Requires minimum 8KB free user memory
- Recommended settings: 19200 baud rate, no parity, 1 stop bit, XMODEM synchronization
- Programs must begin and end with "%"
- Data rate must be fast enough to prevent tool stalling during cuts
- Access via pressing MDI twice

The page includes example DNC program text and display screens showing the waiting and confirmation states.

# HAAS AUTOMATION VF SERIES CONTROL BOOK

**Title:** HAAS AUTOMATION VF SERIES CONTROL BOOK

**Date:** January 2004

## Table of Contents Summary

The manual covers control operation, power management, keyboard functions, various display modes, operation modes (Edit, Memory, MDI, DNC, Handle Jog, Zero Return, List Program), and programming features including the Advanced Editor and Quick Code systems. Additional sections address tool setup, program restart, input/output operations, and control tips.

## Display Screen Layout

The control features multiple integrated displays accessible through mode selection:

- **Program Display** - Shows active programs with review and background edit capabilities
- **Position Display** - Multiple pages showing position (Position, Pos-Oper, Pos-Work, Pos-Machine, Pos-ToGo)
- **Offset Display** - Tool length, radius/diameter, wear offsets, and work offsets
- **Current Commands Display** - Program verification, current commands, operation timers, macro variables, maintenance, tool life, and tool load monitoring
- **Help/Calculator Display** - Trigonometry, circular calculations, milling/tapping data, tangent calculators, decimal charts
- **Graphics Display** - Visual program representation
- **Parameter/Diagnostics Display** - Machine settings and diagnostic data with real-time clock
- **Alarms/Messages Display** - System alerts and miscellaneous control messages

## Pendant Keyboard Layout

The control panel includes:

**Mode Selection Keys:** EDIT, MEM, MDI/DNC, HANDLE JOG, ZERO RET, LIST PROG

**Numeric/Alpha Keys:** Standard 0-9 keypad with special characters (@, :, %, $, !, *, etc.) and letter keys

**Cursor Keys:** Arrow up, down, left, right for navigation

**Override Controls:** Feed rate and spindle speed adjustment buttons with +10%, -10%, and 100% settings

**Jog Keys:** Directional axis movement (+X, -X, +Y, -Y, +Z, -Z, +A, -A, +B, -B)

**Function Keys:** F1-F4 providing context-sensitive operations

**Display Selection:** PRGRM, POSIT, OFSET, CURNT COMDS, HELP, PARAM DGNOS buttons

**Operation Controls:** CYCLE START, FEED HOLD, RESET, SPINDLE ON/OFF, COOLANT ON/OFF buttons

# HAAS Classic Control (CHC) — UI reference for a lookalike trainer

**Terminology first:** what you're describing is officially the **Classic Haas Control (CHC)**, in service from the late 1980s until the **Next Generation Control (NGC)** replaced it (CHC machines are roughly 2016 and older). Getting this name right matters because most current Haas documentation online describes NGC, and several sources conflate the two.

## 0. One important correction up front: the "green screen"

The green is a **display-hardware artifact, not a UI theme**. Early VF-series machines used a **monochrome CRT driven off an MGA-style 9-pin monochrome video signal** (essentially IBM PC monochrome). Those tubes shipped with **green, amber, or white phosphor**, so a given machine was green-on-black or amber-on-black depending on the tube. Later CHC machines moved to a color LCD (10-inch CRT-to-LCD retrofit kits are still sold, and they offer a rotary switch to pick among three monochrome colors to preserve the original look).

On the color CHC, screen color is a user setting: **Setting 198 "Background Color", range 0–255, default 235**, which sets the background of **inactive display panes**. Setting 199 is the backlight timer. There is a hidden color-chart screen reachable through Settings → Alarms → Debug that displays the full 256-color palette, documented by CAMInstructor.

**Practical implication for your trainer:** you have two defensible looks. Either the **monochrome-CRT look** (single phosphor color on black, one fixed-width font, no color coding at all — this is the authentic "green screen" that older students will recognize), or the **color-LCD CHC look** (dark background, white text, inverse-video highlight on the selected field, red alarms). Do not build the NGC look: white/light background, a top status bar split into mode/network/time, tabbed Current Commands, and "active pane has a white background" are all **NGC** behaviors that search results will wrongly hand you as if they were classic.

## 1. Display key group (8 keys, top-center of keypad)

Multiple presses of a key cycle through its sub-screens; PAGE UP / PAGE DOWN moves between pages within a screen.

| Key | What it shows |
|---|---|
| **PRGRM/CONVRS** | Currently selected program. In EDIT mode, press twice for Quick Code, three times for Visual Quick Code. From most modes it jumps to the edit pane of the active program. |
| **POSIT** | Machine axis positions; PAGE UP/DOWN cycles the four position formats as enlarged displays. |
| **OFSET** | Press once for tool offsets (length geometry, radius offsets, wear offsets, coolant position); press twice (or PAGE UP) for work offsets. |
| **CURNT COMDS** | Current program details (G, M, H, T codes), spindle load, and axis positions while the program runs. Ten pages via PAGE UP/DOWN. |
| **ALARM/MESGS** | Three alarm screens (current alarms, alarm history, alarm viewer with descriptions and search-by-number); press twice for the operator Messages screen. |
| **PARAM/DGNOS** | Machine parameters on first press, diagnostics on second. Service-oriented. |
| **SETNG/GRAPH** | Settings on first press, Graphics (visual dry run) on second. |
| **HELP/CALC** | Built-in manual pages plus machining calculators. |

**Pages behind each key** (from the 2004 VF-Series Control Book's own section naming, which is the most authentic CHC page vocabulary):

- **Program Display** → Program Review, Background Edit
- **Position Display** → Position (combined), **Pos-Oper**, **Pos-Work**, **Pos-Mach**, **Pos-To Go**
- **Offset Display** → tool offsets, work zero offsets
- **Current Commands** → Program Command Check, Current Display Command, Operation Timers, Macro Variables, Maintenance, Tool Life, Tool Load. Later CHC software adds Axis Load and a real-time clock/date page; Operation Timers shows **Power-On Time, Cycle Start Time, Feed Cutting Time**.
- **Help** → Help, Calculator Help (trig, circular, milling/tapping data, tangent), Decimal Chart Help
- **Graphics Display**
- **Parameter Display, Diagnostics Display, Real-Time Clock**
- **Alarms Display, Message Display, Miscellaneous Control Messages**

## 2. Mode keys and the sub-key block under each

Six mode keys. **The current mode is displayed on the top line of the screen.** Haas groups them into three functional families: **Setup** (ZERO RET, HAND JOG), **Edit** (EDIT, MDI/DNC, LIST PROG), and **Operation** (MEM). Each mode key heads a horizontal "keyline" of sub-keys that only apply in that mode — this row-per-mode structure is the single most characteristic thing about the Haas keypad and worth reproducing exactly.

- **EDIT** — "Selects edit mode. This mode is used to edit programs in control's memory." Sub-keys: **INSERT, ALTER, DELETE, UNDO**.
- **MEM** — "Selects the memory mode. This page displays the current program that is selected in the list of programs." Sub-keys: **SINGLE BLOCK, DRY RUN, OPT STOP, BLOCK DELETE**.
- **MDI/DNC** — "MDI mode is the 'Manual Data Entry' mode where a program can be written but it is not entered into memory." Second press enters DNC. Sub-keys: **COOLNT, ORIENT SPINDLE, ATC FWD, ATC REV**.
- **HANDLE JOG** — "Selects axis jogging mode .0001, .1 - 0.0001 inches (metric 0.001mm) for each division on the jog handle. For dry run, .1 inches/min." The four increment keys are **dual-labeled**: the top number is the jog increment per handle division (.0001 / .001 / .01 / .1 inch) and the bottom number is the dry-run feedrate (.1 / 1. / 10. / 100. in/min).
- **ZERO RET** — "Selects Zero Return mode, which displays axis location in four different categories, they are; Operator, Work G54, Machine and Dist (distance) to go." Sub-keys: **ALL** ("Returns all axes to machine zero"), **ORIGIN** ("Sets selected displays and timers to zero"), **SINGL** ("Returns one axis to machine zero"), **HOME G28** ("Returns all axes to machine zero in rapid motion"; entering an axis letter first homes just that axis).
- **LIST PROG** — "Displays the programs stored in the control." Sub-keys: **SELECT PROG** ("Makes the highlighted program, in the program list, the current program"), **SEND** ("Transmits programs out the RS-232 serial port"), **RECV** ("Receives programs from the RS-232 serial port"), **ERASE PROG** ("Erases the highlighted program in Memory mode or the entire program when in MDI mode").

### Operator flow

**Power-up:** press POWER ON → self-diagnostics → Messages or Alarms screen appears → typically alarm **102 SERVOS OFF** is present → press RESET a couple of times → press **POWER UP/RESTART** (automatic motion begins; it also clears 102) → axes home → **the Current Commands page is displayed and the machine is ready**.

**Run a program:** LIST PROG → cursor to the program → SELECT PROG → MEM → CYCLE START. FEED HOLD pauses feed but not the spindle. Setting 36 enables mid-program restart. Run-Stop-Jog-Continue lets the operator interrupt, jog away, and resume.

**Graphics dry run:** load a program, be in MEM or MDI, press SETNG/GRAPH twice, then CYCLE START. Screen regions: a central **tool path window** (X/Y, dotted lines = rapid, solid = feed, X marks = drill cycle locations); a **locator window** in the lower right that toggles with **F4** between the full table area with current tool position and four lines of executing code; a horizontal **Z-axis part-zero line** bar whose shading shows Z depth; **F3** opens a position window with all enabled axes, scaling, and simulated tool number; **F2** enables zoom, driven by PAGE DOWN / arrows / PAGE UP.

**DNC (drip feed):** press MDI/DNC twice. Requires Parameter 57 bit 18 and Setting 55; needs ≥8KB free user memory; recommended 19200 baud, no parity, 1 stop bit, XMODEM; the program must begin and end with `%`. Then CYCLE START.

## 3. Keypad groups

The manual is explicit: *"The keyboard is broken up into eight sections: Function Keys, Jog Keys, Override Keys, Display Keys, Cursor Keys, Alpha Keys, Mode Keys and Number Keys."* Outside those eight sit the reset/power keys, EMERGENCY STOP, CYCLE START, FEED HOLD, the jog handle, and the spindle load meter.

**Function keys (upper left):** F1–F4, context-dependent on mode. Alongside them the setup keys: **TOOL OFSET MESUR** (records the tool length offset), **NEXT TOOL** (selects the next tool from the changer during setup), **TOOL RELEASE** (releases the tool in MDI, ZERO RET, or HANDLE JOG modes), **PART ZERO SET** (automatically enters work coordinate offsets).

**Override keys (lower left):**
- Feedrate: **-10%**, **100%**, **+10%**. Feedrate can be varied 0%–999% of programmed.
- Spindle: **-10%**, **100%**, **+10%**. Ineffective during G74 and G84 tapping.
- **HANDLE CNTRL FEED** and **HANDLE CNTRL SPIN** put the jog handle in charge of feed / spindle in ±1% increments.
- Spindle direction: **CW**, **CCW**, **STOP** — usable at a Single Block stop or during Feed Hold.
- Rapid: **5%**, **25%**, **50%**, **100%** (caps G00 moves).
- Settings 19, 20, 21 lock out feedrate, spindle, and rapid overrides respectively; Setting 32 governs coolant override.

**Jog keys:** **+X/-X, +Y/-Y, +Z/-Z, +A/-A, +B/-B**; **JOG LOCK** (continuous jog to travel limit until released); **CHIP FWD / CHIP STOP / CHIP REV**; **CLNT UP / CLNT DOWN** (programmable coolant spigot); **AUX CLNT** (through-spindle coolant, toggled in MDI); **COOLNT**. On five-axis mills, SHIFT + the A jog keys selects the B axis.

**Cursor keys:** **HOME** (top item / first block), **END** (bottom item / last block), **PAGE UP / PAGE DOWN** (change display or scroll a page of program), and the four arrows (select editable items, move within a field, scroll settings; right arrow also pans the graphics zoom window).

**Alpha keys (bottom center):** A–Z plus **EOB** (end-of-block, prints as `;`), parentheses `( )` for comments (must be paired), forward slash `/` (block delete and macro division), square brackets `[ ]` (macro functions), and **SHIFT** for the characters printed in the upper-left of each key. Default entry is uppercase; hold SHIFT for lowercase.

**Numeric keys (bottom right):** 0–9, minus sign, decimal point, **CANCEL** ("used to delete the last character entered"), **SPACE** ("used to format comments placed into programs or in the message area"), and **WRITE/ENTER** ("general purpose enter key").

**Reset/power keys (upper left):** **POWER ON** (green) / **POWER OFF** (red), **POWER UP/RESTART**, **RESET** (stops all motion, puts the program cursor at the top), **TOOL CHANGER RESTORE**. Lathes add **AUTO OFF**.

**Input buffer:** the data-entry area in the **lower-left corner of the screen**; keystrokes appear there before being committed with WRITE/ENTER or a function key.

## 4. Position display

Four readouts, all four visible simultaneously on the combined POSITION page, with PAGE UP/DOWN or the up/down arrows scrolling to each as an enlarged single display:

- **OPERATOR** — *"This display is used to show the distance the operator has jogged any of the axes. This does not represent the actual distance the axis is from machine zero. Axes can be zeroed by selecting an axis (X, Y or Z) and pressing the Origin key."*
- **WORK G54** — position relative to the active work coordinate offset. This is the readout an operator watches while setting up and running.
- **MACHINE** — true position referenced to machine zero (home).
- **DIST TO GO** — distance remaining to reach the commanded endpoint of the current move.

A widely used trick worth supporting in a trainer: the operator page doubles as a **DRO** — press POSIT, page to the operator screen, key an axis letter and a value, then press ORIGIN from the Zero Ret keyline to preset that axis readout.

## 5. Offsets

**Tool offsets page (OFSET, first press).** Columns: tool number, **tool length geometry**, **tool length wear**, **tool radius geometry**, **tool radius wear**, **flutes**, **actual diameter**, and coolant position on machines with the programmable spigot.

**Work zero offset page (OFSET twice, or PAGE UP).** X, Y, Z (and rotary axes) for each work coordinate: **G52**, **G54–G59**, and the extended set. Note a version difference that matters if you're targeting a specific vintage: older CHC software lists **G110–G129**; **G154 P1–P99** arrived with software 12.02 (October 2002) and **G154 P1–P20 address the same registers as G110–G129**. Newer software stops displaying the G110–G129 labels and shows only the P numbers. Setting 157 controls offset display format; Setting 156 saves offsets with the program.

**Entry method** (this is the fiddly bit students get wrong, so model it faithfully): highlight the field, type a number, then
- **F1** — write the typed value into the offset,
- **F2** — write the typed value as a negative,
- **WRITE/ENTER** — *add* the typed value to the existing value (this is how wear is dialed in),
- **ORIGIN** — zero the highlighted value.

**Automatic entry during setup:** **TOOL OFSET MESUR** enters the present Z-axis location into the highlighted tool length offset. **PART ZERO SET** automatically writes the current work coordinate offset during part setup. **NEXT TOOL** indexes to the next tool so the operator can repeat the touch-off loop.

The standard student setup sequence is: HANDLE JOG with an edge finder to establish X and Y → PART ZERO SET into G54 → for each tool, jog Z down to the part top → TOOL OFSET MESUR → NEXT TOOL → repeat → proof in Graphics → run in MEM.

## 6. Screen layout details I could verify

Verbatim layout facts from the manuals, useful for pane sizing:

- The **CURNT COMDS** display shows **fifteen lines of the current program** alongside modal program values and axis positions — so the program pane on that page is a fixed 15 rows.
- The **Program Command Check page** (first Current Commands page) shows **spindle speed as three values — Programmed, Commanded, and Actual** — plus spindle direction (CW / CCW / stopped), transmission gear position, and axis coordinates selectable with the cursor keys.
- A **smaller version of the Active Codes display is embedded in the MEM and MDI mode screens**, which is why the run screen has a compact modal-code block beside the program text.
- The mode name appears on the **top line**; the input buffer sits **lower-left**; selection is by **inverse-video highlight** (there is no mouse, no tabs, no icons).

I could not find an authoritative pane-by-pane, pixel-level description of the CHC MEM run screen in text form — Haas never published one (the pane/tab/active-pane language exists only in the NGC manual), and the 2004 VF-Series Control Book's screen figures are scanned images with no OCR text layer. If you want the run screen exactly right, the reliable move is to work from photographs of a CHC pendant in MEM mode rather than from prose, or to spend an hour with the Tooling U 250 course which is built around annotated CHC screenshots.

## 7. Existing simulators and trainers

- **Haas Control Simulator (Standard and Premium)** — Haas's own desktop unit: a **real, full-function Haas control panel and keypad** in a benchtop enclosure, ~$2,000 list. Includes simulated graphic dry run, tool length measurement, work offsets, true DNC, and VPS, and **can be mirrored to a computer or mobile device and projected for classroom display**. Current units ship with NGC; units sold before ~2015 ran the classic control, and used ones are common in schools — worth knowing because your students may have seen one.
- **SwanSoft SSCNC (Nanjing Swansoft)** — PC training simulator with a dedicated **HAAS VF** module; the suite covers 25 CNC brands, 119 controllers, and 273 operation panels, with a teacher-facing SSCNC Server that receives students' operations in real time. This is the closest existing thing to what you're building, and the most common CNC-lab alternative to real iron.
- **Predator Virtual CNC** — Haas control emulation aimed at verification/backplotting rather than operator training.
- **Tooling U-SME course series** — not software, but a well-structured CHC curriculum you can mirror for lesson sequencing: 250 (Mill Classic Control Panel Overview), 260 (Entering Offsets), 270 (Locating Program Zero), 280 (Program Execution), 256/265 (lathe equivalents), and 111 (Classic vs Next Generation). Their glossaries are the cleanest per-key definitions available for free.
- **No open-source web clone of the classic Haas UI exists.** I checked GitHub specifically; the projects that surface (cncwebsim, webgcode, OpenDNC) are grbl-based simulators or DNC transfer tools with no Haas UI. Your trainer would be the first of its kind in the open, which is a point in favor of building it.

Eight display keys sit top-center of the keypad. Repeated presses cycle sub-screens; PAGE UP/DOWN moves between pages within a screen.

**POSIT** — four readouts, all visible together on the combined page, each also available enlarged via PAGE UP/DOWN. Classic page names are **Position, Pos-Oper, Pos-Work, Pos-Mach, Pos-To Go**.
- *Operator*: "the distance the operator has jogged any of the axes. This does not represent the actual distance the axis is from machine zero. Axes can be zeroed by selecting an axis (X, Y or Z) and pressing the Origin key."
- *Work G54*: position relative to the active work offset — what the operator watches when running.
- *Machine*: position referenced to machine home.
- *Dist To Go*: distance remaining in the current move.
Doubles as a DRO: on the operator page, key an axis letter and a value, then ORIGIN.

**OFSET** — press once for the tool offset table, twice (or PAGE UP) for work offsets.
- Tool page columns: tool number, tool length geometry, length wear, tool radius geometry, radius wear, flutes, actual diameter, coolant position.
- Work page: X/Y/Z (plus rotaries) per coordinate — G52, G54–G59, then G110–G129 on older software or G154 P1–P99 on later (P1–P20 are the same registers as G110–G129; newer software shows only the P numbers).
- Entry: type a value, then **F1** = set, **F2** = set negative, **WRITE/ENTER** = add to the existing value, **ORIGIN** = zero it. **TOOL OFSET MESUR** writes the current Z into the highlighted tool length; **PART ZERO SET** writes the current position into the highlighted work offset.

**PRGRM/CONVRS** — the currently selected program as editable text. In EDIT mode, a second press enters Quick Code, a third Visual Quick Code.

**CURNT COMDS** — ten pages: Program Command Check, Current Display Command, Operation Timers (Power-On Time, Cycle Start Time, Feed Cutting Time), Macro Variables, Maintenance, Tool Life, Tool Load, plus axis load and a clock/date page on later software. The Program Command Check page shows **spindle speed as three values — Programmed, Commanded, Actual** — plus direction (CW/CCW/stopped), gear position, and axis coordinates selectable with cursor keys. This page carries **fifteen lines of the current program** beside the modal values, so budget a 15-row program pane. A **condensed Active Codes block is embedded in the MEM and MDI screens** — that's the modal-code panel on the run screen.

**ALARM/MESGS** — three alarm screens (current alarms, alarm history, alarm viewer with text and search-by-number), then a second press for the operator Messages screen, which is free text, survives power cycles, and is what you see at startup when no alarm is active.

**SETNG/GRAPH** — settings list on the first press, Graphics on the second. Graphics regions: central tool path window (dotted = rapid, solid = feed, X = drill location); **locator window** lower-right, toggled by **F4** between the full table view and four lines of executing code; a horizontal **Z part-zero bar** shaded to show depth; **F3** opens a position window; **F2** enables zoom driven by PAGE DOWN / arrows / PAGE UP. Needs a loaded program and MEM or MDI mode, then CYCLE START.

# 2. Mode keys and flow

The mode name shows on the **top line**. Each mode key heads a horizontal keyline of sub-keys that only apply in that mode — reproducing that row-per-mode structure matters more than anything else on the keypad.

| Mode | Sub-keys | Flow |
|---|---|---|
| **EDIT** | INSERT, ALTER, DELETE, UNDO | Edits programs already in memory. |
| **MEM** | SINGLE BLOCK, DRY RUN, OPT STOP, BLOCK DELETE | Shows the currently selected program; CYCLE START runs it, FEED HOLD pauses feed but not the spindle. |
| **MDI/DNC** | COOLNT, ORIENT SPINDLE, ATC FWD, ATC REV | Type blocks and CYCLE START without storing to memory; ERASE PROG clears the MDI buffer. Second press = DNC. |
| **HANDLE JOG** | .0001/.1, .001/1., .01/10., .1/100. | Dual-labeled keys: top number is inches per handle division, bottom is dry-run feedrate in in/min. |
| **ZERO RET** | ALL, ORIGIN, SINGL, HOME G28 | "displays axis location in four different categories… Operator, Work G54, Machine and Dist (distance) to go." ALL returns all axes to machine zero; SINGL one axis; ORIGIN "Sets selected displays and timers to zero"; HOME G28 rapids all axes home, or one axis if you type its letter first. |
| **LIST PROG** | SELECT PROG, SEND, RECV, ERASE PROG | SELECT PROG "Makes the highlighted program, in the program list, the current program." ERASE PROG "Erases the highlighted program in Memory mode or the entire program when in MDI mode." |

Haas groups these as **Setup** (ZERO RET, HAND JOG), **Edit** (EDIT, MDI/DNC, LIST PROG), **Operation** (MEM).

Power-up sequence: POWER ON → self-test → Messages or Alarms screen → alarm **102 SERVOS OFF** → RESET twice → **POWER UP/RESTART** homes all axes → the Current Commands page appears and the machine is ready. Normal run: LIST PROG → cursor to program → SELECT PROG → MEM → CYCLE START.

# 3. EDIT mode specifics

**Yes — the cursor selects a whole g-code word, not a character.** Cursor keys "move up or down one item, block, or field," and the operator interacts with a single piece of code (cursor highlighting), a block, or multiple blocks (block selection). The highlighted word is shown in inverse video. There is no character-level caret in the classic editor.

Verbatim behavior of the four sub-keys:

- **INSERT** — "Pressing this button will enter commands into the program in front of the cursor. This button will also insert the text from the clipboard to the current cursor location, and is also used to copy blocks of code in a program."
- **ALTER** — "Pressing this button will change the highlighted command or text to the newly entered commands or text. This button will also change the highlighted variables to the text stored in the clipboard, or move a selected block to another location."
- **DELETE** — "Deletes the item that the cursor is on, or deletes a selected program block."
- **UNDO** — "Undoes up to the last 9 edit changes, and deselects a highlighted block."

So the editing loop is: cursor to a word → type the replacement into the input buffer (bottom-left) → ALTER to replace it, or INSERT to add it ahead of the cursor, or DELETE to remove it. **CANCEL** backspaces a character in the input buffer, and also cancels a highlighted block during a block edit. Note that each of the three keys has a second, clipboard/block meaning — that dual role is genuine classic-control behavior and worth implementing if you want block copy/move to work.

# 4. Colour scheme — with a correction

**The green is display hardware, not a UI theme.** Early VF machines used a monochrome CRT on an MGA-style 9-pin monochrome signal, shipped with **green, amber, or white phosphor** depending on the tube. That is where "green screen Haas" comes from. Later classic-control machines used a colour LCD, and CRT-to-LCD retrofit kits still sold today include a rotary switch to pick among three monochrome colours precisely to preserve that look.

What I could verify about colour on the colour-LCD classic control is thin, and I'd rather flag that than invent a palette: **Setting 198 "Background Color", range 0–255, default 235**, sets the background of *inactive* display panes; Setting 199 is the backlight timer; and a hidden colour-chart screen reachable through Settings → Alarms → Debug shows the full 256-colour palette. Haas published a Background Color Reference Table, but it's a colour swatch image with no text layer, so I couldn't extract RGB values.

I did not find any authoritative per-pane colour specification, and I'd treat anything you find describing "the active pane has a white background," a top status bar split into mode/network/time, or tabbed Current Commands as **Next Generation Control**, not classic — several sources conflate them and it would send your UI in the wrong visual direction.

My recommendation: build the **monochrome-CRT look** — one phosphor colour on black, a single fixed-width font, no colour coding, inverse-video for the highlighted word or field, everything laid out on a fixed character grid. It's what students recognize as "the old Haas," it's unambiguously period-correct, and it sidesteps the palette question entirely. If you want the colour-LCD variant later, the honest way to get the palette right is photographs of a real pendant rather than documentation.
